target: AG1’s claim that school dissections mostly use already-dead animals and fetal pigs that would otherwise be landfill waste.
objection: Most school dissection animals are not merely repurposed dead specimens; AG2 argues that approximately 99% are caught in the wild, so dissection typically involves harming wild animals and reducing local biodiversity.

target: AG1’s claim that real-animal dissection provides educational benefits that justify its use.
objection: Synthetic models and computer simulations can teach the relevant concepts effectively, and students learn just as well or better with these alternatives, so real animals are not educationally necessary.

target: AG1’s implication that dissection is educationally justified because it supports biology and medical training.
objection: Animal dissection is not required by AP Biology or NGSS, and no U.S. or Canadian medical schools use animals for physician training, so it is unnecessary for the relevant learning goals.

target: AG1’s overall conclusion that students should dissect animals in biology class.
objection: Because most dissections allegedly depend on harming wild animals and the educational aims can be met with alternatives, students should not dissect animals.

target: AG2’s claim that most dissections involve wild-caught animals and therefore harm biodiversity.
objection: In school biology dissection, over 98% of animals used were already deceased and fetal pigs are meat-industry byproducts, so the “most dissections harm wild animals” framing is not generally accurate.

target: AG2’s claim that alternatives can teach the educational goals of dissection just as well or better.
objection: Even if models and simulations teach some concepts, they do not fully replicate the tactile, hands-on procedural experience needed to develop fine motor skills, hand-eye coordination, and associated critical thinking.

target: AG2’s assumption that AP/NGSS non-mandatory status and lack of medical-school use show dissection is unnecessary.
objection: Whether dissection is mandated by standards or used in medical training does not determine its educational value in school biology; schools can include activities that build skills and engagement beyond minimum requirements.

target: AG1’s argument that fetal pig specimens are just byproducts and therefore the supply chain should not matter.
objection: Even if fetal pigs are marketed as byproducts, buying them still supports a meat-industry supply chain that is inhumane and environmentally harmful, so the practice is not harm-free.

target: AG1’s claim that using byproduct specimens for dissection is a productive and acceptable use of materials.
objection: Because dissection materials come from an inhumane and environmentally harmful supply chain, schools should not require dissection when those harms can be avoided.

target: AG1’s claim that using byproduct specimens for dissection is productive because it repurposes materials.
objection: Synthetic models and computer simulations can replace real-animal dissection, letting schools avoid the harmful animal-supply chain entirely.

target: AG2’s assertion that buying dissection specimens causes additional slaughter beyond what would happen for meat production anyway.
objection: School dissection usually uses animals already dead or meat-industry byproducts, so dissection demand does not meaningfully create additional slaughter beyond existing meat production.

target: AG2’s broader claim that the harms of industrial animal agriculture are a strong reason to reject school dissection.
objection: Those upstream harms do not strongly justify rejecting classroom dissection when the classroom activity uses already-dead/byproduct animals and can reduce waste by repurposing them.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection demand increases slaughter in the meat industry.
objection: Dissection orders are not the main driver of meat production, so stopping school purchases would not materially reduce meat slaughter or the associated byproducts.

target: AG2’s weak-negation assumption that using dissection demand does not cause additional animal slaughter beyond meat production.
objection: That assumption is false because the meat supply is driven primarily by meat demand, not school dissection purchases, so removing school demand would not meaningfully change slaughter levels.

target: AG2’s claim that schools should avoid dissection because alternatives exist and the byproducts would otherwise be landfilled.
objection: Avoiding dissection would not meaningfully reduce upstream harms if the byproducts are produced anyway; it would mainly change what happens to those byproducts, while dissection can repurpose them productively.

target: AG1’s claim that avoiding dissection does not meaningfully reduce harms because byproducts would be produced anyway.
objection: If schools stop buying dissection specimens, demand for those byproducts falls at the margin, so avoiding dissection can reduce disposal burdens and the demand that supports the supply chain.

target: AG1’s claim that byproduct use makes dissection acceptable because the upstream harms are unavoidable.
objection: Even if the byproducts would exist anyway, schools should still avoid dissection when non-animal alternatives can meet the educational goals and reduce harmful demand.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is justified because the specimens are already dead and the activity does not add slaughter.
objection: The specimens still come from slaughter and processing upstream, so encouraging schools to buy them supports a harmful supply chain even if the lesson itself does not directly kill animals.

target: AG1’s claim that alternatives do not make dissection educationally unnecessary.
objection: Synthetic models and computer simulations can teach the relevant concepts well enough that real-animal dissection is not needed to meet biology learning goals.

target: AG1’s overall conclusion that classroom dissection should be allowed because it has educational benefits and low incremental harm.
objection: When a harmful practice is avoidable and alternatives meet the learning goals, it is not justified to require or encourage the harmful practice.

target: AG1’s claim that school dissection mainly uses already-dead animals rather than harming wildlife.
objection: AG2 again counters that most dissection animals are wild-caught, so school dissection typically harms wild populations and biodiversity rather than merely repurposing dead animals.

target: AG1’s claim that standards or medical training practices do not matter because dissection has intrinsic educational value.
objection: AP Biology/NGSS do not require dissection and U.S./Canadian medical schools do not use animals for physician training, so dissection is not necessary for the relevant educational objectives.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection should be kept because the activity is useful and educational.
objection: Since the same learning outcomes can be achieved with non-animal alternatives and the practice imposes avoidable environmental and animal-supply harms, requiring dissection is unjustified.

target: AG1’s claim that real-animal dissection should be encouraged because it is a productive use of byproducts.
objection: School dissection typically involves wild-caught animals and biodiversity harm, so it is not simply a benign use of already-deceased materials.

target: AG1’s implication that dissection is necessary or required for biology and medical education.
objection: Animal dissection is not required by AP Biology, NGSS, or U.S./Canadian medical training, so it is not necessary for the relevant learning objectives.

target: AG1’s claim that schools should encourage dissection because it is educationally beneficial.
objection: If an activity is not necessary for the learning objectives and typically causes inhumane or environmentally harmful impacts, schools should not encourage or require it.

target: AG1’s claim that using already-deceased or byproduct specimens makes classroom dissection harm-free.
objection: Even when specimens are described as already dead or as byproducts, dissection still depends on the same harmful animal-supply chain that produced them, so the practice is not harm-free.

target: AG1’s claim that alternatives cannot replace the educational value of real dissection.
objection: Synthetic models and computer simulations can teach dissection-related concepts effectively and may let students learn just as well or better without using animals.

target: AG1’s conclusion that dissection should be encouraged because it repurposes byproducts.
objection: When a harmful practice is avoidable and alternatives meet the relevant learning goals, encouraging or requiring the harmful practice is unjustified.

target: AG1’s claim that repurposing byproducts makes dissection acceptable and not harmful.
objection: The byproducts only exist because of slaughter and processing upstream, so using them in dissection does not eliminate the inhumane and environmentally harmful harms tied to their production.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection can be justified because it uses already-dead/byproduct materials.
objection: The underlying animal-agriculture supply chain is inhumane and bad for the environment, so the fact that specimens are byproducts does not make the practice harm-free.

target: AG1’s claim that schools can keep using dissection specimens without causing meaningful upstream harm.
objection: Buying and using dissection specimens supports the upstream slaughter and processing that produce them, so it does not eliminate the harms caused by the supply chain.

target: AG1’s conclusion that students should be encouraged to dissect animals.
objection: Because the educational objectives can be met without dissection and the practice supports a harmful supply chain, students should not be encouraged or required to dissect animals.
